facts.title: What business analysis is
facts.text: Business analysis is the work of understanding a need and recommending a change that has value. The BABOK Guide is IIBA's published standard for that practice. This lab summarizes the public structure. It does not replace the guide.

facts.title: Who does the work
facts.text: The guide's contents include a section on who a business analyst is. In practice the title varies: business analyst, business systems analyst, product owner, or consultant. The title is less important than whether someone is accountable for the need, the stakeholders, and the change.

facts.title: Core concept model
facts.text: The knowledge hub lists the Business Analysis Core Concept Model. Study it as six linked ideas: change, need, solution, stakeholder, value, and context. A sentence that names a solution but not the need is incomplete. Change: the act of transformation. Need: a problem or opportunity.

facts.title: Requirements and designs
facts.text: The guide treats requirements and designs as related, not as two sealed boxes. A requirement states a condition or capability. A design describes a solution. The same statement can be read as either, depending on who consumes it. Say which reading you intend.

facts.title: Requirements classification
facts.text: A useful study split, following the guide's classification schema, is business, stakeholder, solution, and transition. Solution requirements are often split again into functional behavior and non-functional quality. Label the class so reviewers know what 'done' means.

facts.title: Business analyst and project manager
facts.text: A project manager is accountable for the delivery plan: time, cost, and coordination. A business analyst is accountable for whether the change is worth making and whether the result meets the need. Teams combine the roles. They should not pretend the roles are the same decision.

facts.title: Business analyst and product owner
facts.text: The 2020 Scrum Guide places a Product Owner on the Scrum Team with Developers and a Scrum Master, and it lists the Product Backlog as an artifact. A business analyst may support that backlog or, in some teams, hold the Product Owner accountability. Holding both without saying so hides the decision rights.

facts.title: Need before solution
facts.text: Start from the outcome a stakeholder can observe. A tool name, a screen, or a vendor is a solution hypothesis. Write the need in a sentence that would still make sense if the tool changed.

facts.title: Stakeholders
facts.text: The guide lists stakeholders as a core topic. Map who is affected, who decides, who pays, and who can block. A person with high influence and low interest still needs a plan. Update the map when the change moves.

facts.title: Scope in one paragraph
facts.text: Scope is the boundary of the change: what is in, what is out, and what is unknown. Write the out-of-scope list. It prevents a later argument from being treated as a surprise.

facts.title: Assumptions and constraints
facts.text: An assumption is something you proceed with while it remains unproven. A constraint is a limit you do not get to choose, such as a law, a date, or a system you must keep. Review assumptions on a cadence. A false assumption is a risk.

facts.title: Value is contextual
facts.text: Value is not a single number. It depends on which stakeholder and which context you name. A faster call handling time can be value for an operations lead and a loss of care for a customer. State both.

facts.title: Where the practice sits
facts.text: Business analysis touches product ownership, project delivery, process improvement, data analysis, architecture, and change management. The BABOK Guide is the core reference in this lab. Neighboring guides are cited only where a page opened.

facts.title: Sister roles
facts.text: Product manager, product owner, project manager, process analyst, data analyst, business architect, and quality analyst share techniques with business analysis. Ask which decisions each role owns on this initiative. Shared techniques do not mean shared authority.

facts.title: Bridges to other labs
facts.text: Contact-center work needs the same elicitation and acceptance habits, plus queue, channel, and quality measures. AI agent work needs a human review step on any requirement the model drafted. This lab links those topics. It does not claim a vendor implementation.

facts.title: Future hooks
facts.text: Useful next studies are decision modeling, process mining, and evaluation of AI-assisted analysis. Each is introduced here only as far as a public source opened. Deeper vendor features stay marked to be confirmed.

facts.title: Planning and monitoring
facts.text: This knowledge area covers how the analysis itself will be run: the approach, stakeholder engagement, governance, information management, and how you will know the analysis work is performing. It is the plan for the analysis, not the plan for the whole project. Plan the business analysis approach. Plan stakeholder engagement.

facts.title: Elicitation and collaboration
facts.text: Prepare, conduct, confirm, communicate, and keep collaboration going. Elicitation is not a single workshop. Confirmation is a separate task so that notes are not mistaken for agreement.

facts.title: Requirements life cycle management
facts.text: Trace, maintain, prioritize, assess changes, and approve. A requirement without a trace to a need and to a test is a rumor. Approval is a recorded decision, not a silent meeting.

facts.title: Strategy analysis
facts.text: Analyze the current state, define a future state, assess risks, and define a change strategy. Strategy work answers why this change, and what we are willing to risk, before the team debates screens.

facts.title: Requirements analysis and design definition
facts.text: Specify and model, verify, validate, define the requirements architecture, define design options, and recommend a solution based on potential value. Verification asks whether the requirement is fit to use. Validation asks whether it is the right requirement.

facts.title: Solution evaluation
facts.text: Measure performance, analyze those measures, assess solution limits, assess enterprise limits, and recommend actions that increase value. Evaluation continues after go-live. The CBAP sample material on the public page makes the same point: limitation assessment happens when the solution is in use in some form.

facts.title: Underlying competencies
facts.text: The guide lists analytical thinking, behavioral characteristics, business knowledge, communication, interaction, and tools and technology. Tools are last on purpose. A diagramming product does not supply the judgment.

facts.title: Technique list
facts.text: The public contents list fifty techniques, from acceptance criteria and backlog management through workshops. Learn the name, the question it answers, and one way it fails. Do not memorize a vendor's menu as if it were the technique.

facts.title: Interviews
facts.text: An interview is a prepared conversation with a purpose, questions, and a written confirmation. Send the notes back. Unconfirmed notes are your memory, not the stakeholder's agreement.

facts.title: Workshops
facts.text: A workshop gathers people who can decide or inform, with an agenda and a record. If the decision maker is absent, record the outcome as a draft.

facts.title: Observation
facts.text: Watch the work. People skip steps they no longer notice. Observation checks what an interview smooths over. Tell people you are observing, unless a formal study design says otherwise and ethics allow it.

facts.title: Document analysis
facts.text: Read the policy, the contract, the ticket history, and the old specification before you ask people to repeat them. Mark the date of each document. Old documents describe a world that may have changed.

facts.title: Prototyping
facts.text: A prototype is a learning tool. Label its fidelity. A polished picture can be mistaken for a promise. Capture which comments changed the requirement.

facts.title: User stories
facts.text: The technique list includes user stories. A common study form is: as a role, I want a capability, so that an outcome. The outcome is the part teams skip. Atlassian publishes a user-story explanation that matches this shape.

facts.title: Use cases and scenarios
facts.text: A use case names an actor and a goal, then the main path and the exceptions. Scenarios are concrete passes through that path. They become tests more easily than a paragraph of features.

facts.title: Process modelling and analysis
facts.text: Process modelling draws how work moves. Process analysis asks where it waits, loops, or fails. Draw the current state before you draw the wish.

facts.title: Data modelling and dictionary
facts.text: A data model names things the business cares about and how they relate. A data dictionary defines each field, including what 'blank' means. Skip the dictionary and two teams will load different meanings into the same column.

facts.title: Non-functional requirements
facts.text: Quality attributes include performance, security, availability, accessibility, and retention. Write a measure. 'Fast' is not a requirement. 'The search returns in under two seconds for the agreed test' can be tested.

facts.title: Business rules
facts.text: A business rule is a decision the organization enforces, such as who may approve a refund. Keep rules separate from process steps so a policy change does not require redrawing every flow.

facts.title: SWOT
facts.text: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats are a snapshot. Strengths and weaknesses are internal. Opportunities and threats are external. A SWOT without a decision attached is a poster.

facts.title: Risk analysis
facts.text: A risk is an uncertain event that would matter if it happened. Write the event, the consequence, and the response you will actually take. A risk register that nobody reviews is a filing exercise.

facts.title: Metrics and KPIs
facts.text: The technique list names metrics and key performance indicators. A KPI needs a definition, a source, a cadence, and a person who acts when it moves. A number without an owner is a dashboard decoration.

facts.title: Vendor assessment
facts.text: Vendor assessment compares options against the need, not against the loudest demo. Separate must-have constraints from scored wishes. Record who scored and when.

facts.title: Business cases
facts.text: A business case recommends a course of action with costs, benefits, risks, and assumptions. If you do not know a figure, mark it unknown. Do not invent a return to make the page look finished.

facts.title: Root cause analysis
facts.text: Ask why the problem happens, more than once, until you reach something the team can change. Stopping at the first cause usually names a person instead of a system.

facts.title: Prioritization
facts.text: Prioritization is a decision about sequence and sacrifice. Name the rule: value, risk, dependency, or compliance. A list where everything is high priority has not been prioritized.

facts.title: Backlog management
facts.text: A backlog is an ordered list of options, not a warehouse of every idea. The Scrum Guide describes a Product Backlog as an artifact. Ordering it is ongoing work.

facts.title: Elicitation methods
facts.text: Choose a method for the question. Interviews go deep with one person. Workshops align a group. Observation checks real work. Surveys reach many people with thin answers. Document analysis starts from what is already written. Say why you picked the method.

facts.title: Stakeholder grid
facts.text: A simple grid places influence on one axis and interest on the other. High influence and high interest people need close work. High influence and low interest people need concise updates. The grid is a hypothesis. Test it.

facts.title: Story and outcome
facts.text: Write the role, the capability, and the outcome. Then add acceptance criteria. Atlassian's user-story material is a public explanation of this shape. A story without a test is a wish.

facts.title: Acceptance criteria in Gherkin
facts.text: Cucumber's Gherkin reference describes scenarios with Given, When, and Then. Given is context. When is the action. Then is the observable result. One scenario, one behavior. Keep the language in the business's words.

facts.title: Traceability
facts.text: Trace a requirement to the need it serves, the design that satisfies it, and the test that demonstrates it. The life-cycle tasks include tracing and assessing change. When a rule changes, the trace tells you what else moves.

facts.title: Traceability matrix
facts.text: A requirements traceability matrix is a table of those links. Columns that help: identifier, statement, source, owner, priority, design reference, test reference, status. A matrix that is not updated is a historical document. Say so.

facts.title: User acceptance
facts.text: Acceptance is a decision by the people who will live with the result, against criteria written earlier. It is not the first time anyone sees the system. Defects found here are either missed criteria or a changed need. Record which.

facts.title: From criteria to tests
facts.text: Each acceptance criterion should suggest at least one test, including the unhappy path. A business analyst does not have to execute every test. They do have to notice when a criterion cannot be tested.

facts.title: Must, should, could, won't
facts.text: Must, should, could, and won't are priority words. Must means the change fails its purpose without it. Won't means not in this scope, on purpose. The DSDM page that documents MoSCoW did not open in the October 2026 check, so it is not linked. To be confirmed: A live DSDM or Agile Business Consortium page for the MoSCoW definition.

facts.title: Quality requirements you can test
facts.text: Pair every quality word with a threshold, a method, and a context. Accessibility can point at WCAG 2.2's quick reference. Do not write 'secure' and walk away.

facts.title: Change control
facts.text: A change request names what moved, why, the impact on scope and tests, and who approved. Assess requirements changes is a life-cycle task. Verbal agreement in a hallway is not a baseline.

facts.title: Baseline and versions
facts.text: A baseline is an agreed version you can compare against later. Keep the previous version. Diff the words. Teams lose arguments when the only copy is the latest edit.

facts.title: BPMN in brief
facts.text: Object Management Group publishes BPMN 2.0. For study, learn events, activities, gateways, and sequence flow. A gateway is a decision, not a task. Label the outgoing paths with conditions a stranger can test.

facts.title: Current state, then future
facts.text: Draw how the work happens this week, including the spreadsheet and the rework. Then draw the proposed state. If you only draw the future, you will miss the step that actually takes the time.

facts.title: UML, used sparingly
facts.text: OMG publishes UML. Use the diagram that answers the question in the room. A use case diagram shows who wants what. An activity diagram shows flow. A sequence diagram shows messages over time. A class diagram shows structure. One diagram, one question.

facts.title: Entity relationships
facts.text: An entity is a thing you store. A relationship states how many of one relate to how many of another. Name the relationship from both directions. 'Customer places order' is clearer than a line with no verb.

facts.title: C4, four levels
facts.text: The C4 model site describes four abstractions: software system, container, component, and code. Start with a system context diagram: the system, the people, and the other systems. Go deeper only where the audience needs it.

facts.title: SIPOC
facts.text: Supplier, input, process, output, customer is a one-page boundary. It is enough to see whether you are looking at the right process before you draw thirty boxes. This is a study scaffold, not a claimed standard text.

facts.title: States
facts.text: State models help when a thing has a life: draft, submitted, approved, rejected. Name the event that causes each move and who may cause it. The technique list includes state modelling.

facts.title: Decisions apart from flow
facts.text: If a gateway contains a policy, lift the policy into a decision with inputs and outputs. The process then stays stable when the policy changes. Decision modelling is on the technique list.

facts.title: Interfaces
facts.text: Interface analysis asks what crosses a boundary: data, a document, or a handoff. For each crossing, name the producer, the consumer, the trigger, and what happens when it fails.

facts.title: Story map
facts.text: A story map places user activities across the top and breaks releases downward. The first horizontal slice should be a thin outcome someone can use, not a layer of database tables.

facts.title: Scrum, from the 2020 guide
facts.text: The Scrum Guide lists three pillars: transparency, inspection, and adaptation. The team accountabilities are Developers, Product Owner, and Scrum Master. Events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective. Artifacts are the Product Backlog, the Sprint Backlog, and the Increment.

facts.title: Product owner accountability
facts.text: Treat the Product Owner as the person who orders the Product Backlog toward value. A business analyst can prepare options and evidence. If several people reorder the backlog, the team does not have a single accountability.

facts.title: PSM and PSPO
facts.text: Scrum.org publishes Professional Scrum assessments. The assessment pages did not open in the 16 October 2026 check, so this lab does not link them and does not state a fee. To be confirmed: Current PSM and PSPO fees and the exact assessment rules on scrum.org.

facts.title: CSPO
facts.text: Scrum Alliance lists Certified Scrum Product Owner on its product owner track, alongside advanced and professional levels. The page opened, but the fee and the course-hour rules did not render in the static check. Do not budget from this lab. To be confirmed: CSPO course price and the eligibility rules shown after the page's scripts run.

facts.title: SAFe POPM
facts.text: Scaled Agile's site opened. The Product Owner / Product Manager course page returned HTTP 429 on 16 October 2026, so it is not linked and no price is copied. SAFe distinguishes product ownership at team level from product management across a larger train. Confirm the current split on their site. To be confirmed: POPM price, duration, and exam rules.

facts.title: Kanban
facts.text: A kanban board makes work visible and limits how much is in progress. Miro publishes a Kanban page that opened. Kanban University's home title loaded on 16 October 2026, but course names and fees did not render, so that site is not linked and no price is copied. To be confirmed: Kanban University course names and fees.

facts.title: Design thinking
facts.text: IDEO's design thinking site opened. Use it as a reminder to spend time with the people who have the problem before you converge on a solution. It is a practice, not a certificate this lab can price.

facts.title: Design sprint
facts.text: Google's Design Sprint Kit opened. A design sprint is a short, structured cycle of understanding, sketching, deciding, prototyping, and testing. It is not the same thing as a Scrum sprint. Say which one you mean.

facts.title: Jobs to be done
facts.text: The Christensen Institute describes Jobs to Be Done as the progress a person is trying to make in a circumstance. Interview for the circumstance and the struggle, not for a feature list. A job story is a study form: when this situation, I want to make this progress, so I can reach this outcome.

facts.title: OKRs
facts.text: Google's re:Work guide introduces objectives and key results. An objective is the direction. Key results are measurable outcomes, not a task list. A business analyst can help a team tell an output from an outcome.

facts.title: SQL for a question
facts.text: PostgreSQL's tutorial introduces SQL as the way to ask a database a question. Learn SELECT, filter, join, and group. You do not need to be the database administrator. You do need to know whether the column you were promised actually exists.

facts.title: Spreadsheets
facts.text: A spreadsheet is often the current system. Before you replace it, learn its formulas, its hidden columns, and who repairs it on Fridays. This note is practice advice. A specific product manual is not cited because none was required for the habit.

facts.title: Conceptual, logical, physical
facts.text: A conceptual model uses business words. A logical model adds keys and cardinality. A physical model adds types and indexes for one database. Do not start at the physical model with stakeholders who came to talk about orders.

facts.title: KPI definition sheet
facts.text: For each indicator write the question it answers, the formula, the grain, the source system, the refresh, the owner, and the threshold for action. HEART, from the Google Research paper on user-centered metrics, is one way to group product measures: happiness, engagement, adoption, retention, and task success.

facts.title: HEART
facts.text: The paper 'Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications' is the public source for the HEART categories. Use the categories as a checklist. Do not invent a benchmark number this lab did not measure.

facts.title: Measures and OKRs
facts.text: A key result that counts tasks completed is usually an output. Prefer a result a customer or the operation can feel. Tie the measure back to the need in the business case.

facts.title: Power BI, as a study topic
facts.text: Microsoft Learn has a page titled What is Power BI. On 16 October 2026 the readable body asked for authorization, so this lab does not describe product features from it. Lucky's notes do not claim Power BI experience. To be confirmed: A publicly readable feature description of Power BI.

facts.title: Tableau, not linked
facts.text: Tableau is a visual analytics product teams use for dashboards. Its public page did not open in the 16 October 2026 check, so it is not linked and no feature is described. This lab does not claim Tableau experience for Lucky. To be confirmed: A Tableau page that opens and can be cited.

facts.title: Process mining
facts.text: The IEEE Task Force on Process Mining site opened. Process mining uses event logs to reconstruct how work actually flowed. It is evidence about the current state. It still needs a person to decide whether the flow is acceptable.

facts.title: Dashboards
facts.text: A dashboard is a decision surface. Lead with the question, then the number, then the breakdown. If a chart does not change a decision, leave it off. Cite the definition of every figure.

facts.title: Jira
facts.text: Atlassian's getting-started guide for Jira opened. Use it to keep work visible: items, states, and owners. The workflow should match the real approval path. Do not add states nobody will use.

facts.title: Confluence
facts.text: Confluence is Atlassian's space for longer pages. A requirement page needs an owner, a status, and a link to the backlog item. A page without a status looks current long after it is not.

facts.title: Azure DevOps boards
facts.text: Microsoft's Azure DevOps backlogs documentation opened. Boards are another place teams order work. The analysis habits are the same as in Jira: one backlog, clear states, and acceptance criteria on the item.

facts.title: Visio
facts.text: Microsoft's Visio support home opened. Visio is a diagramming product teams use for process and system drawings. The drawing is only as good as the labels. Export a copy stakeholders can open.

facts.title: Lucid and BPMN
facts.text: Lucid's BPMN tutorial opened. Use a shared diagram when more than one person must edit. Agree on a small stencil so the file does not become a clip-art board.

facts.title: Miro
facts.text: Miro's Kanban page opened. A board is useful in a workshop because people can move notes. After the workshop, copy the decisions into the system of record. A board that is the only copy will be lost.

facts.title: Figma
facts.text: Figma's home page opened. It is a collaborative design surface teams use for interfaces. Treat a frame as a prototype at a stated fidelity. Comments on a frame are not approved requirements until someone records them as such.

facts.title: Power Platform and Dynamics
facts.text: Microsoft's Power Platform ALM overview and the Dynamics 365 implementation guide both opened. They are relevant when a solution will be configured rather than only described. The business analyst still writes the need, the roles, and the acceptance checks. This is study context, not a claim of delivery experience.

facts.title: Prompt for a draft
facts.text: Ask a model for a draft you can edit: a question list, a stakeholder map, or a first pass at acceptance criteria. Give it the need, the constraint, and the audience. Read every line before it reaches a stakeholder.

facts.title: Human review
facts.text: The analyst remains accountable for the requirement. Check names, numbers, and rules against a source. A fluent paragraph can still be wrong. Keep the source next to the draft.

facts.title: Invented facts
facts.text: Models fill gaps. If the source does not state a fee, a law, or a metric, the draft must say unknown. This lab follows that rule. You should too when you use a model on a real initiative.

facts.title: Agents and omni-channel
facts.text: An agent that talks to a customer is a solution with requirements: what it may say, what it must hand to a person, how it is measured, and how a mistake is reversed. The SRE book's introduction is a public reminder that operations, including handoff, is part of the system.

facts.title: Responsible use
facts.text: Do not paste secrets, customer data, or unpublished financials into a tool whose terms you have not read. Say when a stakeholder is talking to a model. Accessibility and appeal paths still apply.

facts.title: Evaluate the assistant
facts.text: Write a small set of cases before you trust a drafting assistant: a normal case, an edge case, and a case it should refuse. Score it. A demo is not an evaluation.

facts.title: Trace the draft
facts.text: Tag sentences that came from a model until a person checks them. In a traceability matrix, 'model draft, unreviewed' is an honest status.

facts.title: Contact center handoff
facts.text: For a voice or chat agent, specify the moment a person takes over, what context moves with the conversation, and how the customer is not asked to start again. That handoff is a requirement, not a model parameter.

facts.title: Healthcare
facts.text: Healthcare changes often involve privacy, consent, and clinical safety. The HHS HIPAA pages did not open in this check, so they are not linked and the rule text is not paraphrased. HL7's FHIR overview did open. FHIR is a published interoperability standard. Confirm every privacy rule with the organization's compliance owner. To be confirmed: A public HIPAA page that opens, for any privacy paraphrase.

facts.title: Banking
facts.text: Banking analysis pays attention to identity, audit trails, segregation of duties, and retention. This lab does not cite a regulator because no regulator page was opened in the check. Do not invent a control number. Ask the compliance owner which rule applies. To be confirmed: A regulator page for the specific banking control you are studying.

facts.title: Insurance
facts.text: Insurance work turns on the policy, the claim, and the exception. Model those entities before you design a screen. Rating and reserve rules are specialist knowledge. Mark them as sourced from the carrier, not from this lab.

facts.title: Retail
facts.text: Retail changes often involve item, price, inventory, and the path from interest to purchase. Define the grain of 'a sale'. Online and store paths diverge. Write both if both are in scope.

facts.title: Telecom
facts.text: Telecom analysis meets orders, service activation, and faults. Separate the customer-facing promise from the network task. A public TM Forum page was not opened in this check, so it is not linked. To be confirmed: A TM Forum or similar public page for the framework you want to cite.

facts.title: Contact center and CCaaS
facts.text: A contact-center analyst looks at why people contact, which channel they use, how work is queued, and how quality is reviewed. Specify the data a agent or a person needs at the start of the conversation. Vendor product claims stay out unless a page was opened.

facts.title: ERP and CRM
facts.text: Salesforce's CRM page opened. Dynamics 365's implementation guide opened. Both are examples of systems that already contain processes. Fit-gap analysis asks what the product does, what you will configure, and what you will not change. A gap is not automatically a customization.

facts.title: Regulation as a source
facts.text: When a requirement comes from a rule, cite the rule and the version. If you cannot open the text, write 'source not yet attached' rather than a guessed clause. This lab would rather show a gap than a false citation.

facts.title: Discovery
facts.text: Discovery is the work of testing whether you understand the problem. Use interviews, observation, and a small experiment. A discovery output is a clearer need, a rejected idea, or a decision to stop. All three are success.

facts.title: Business case and return
facts.text: List costs, benefits, the timing of each, and the assumptions. If you compute a return, show the formula and the inputs. Unknown inputs stay blank. The technique list includes business cases and financial analysis. This lab states no sample return.

facts.title: Change and ADKAR
facts.text: Prosci's ADKAR page opened and names Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement. A requirement can be built and still fail if people do not know why it exists or cannot perform the new work. Plan the enablement with the solution, not after the outage.

facts.title: Ethics
facts.text: IIBA's certification FAQ says candidates agree to a code of ethical conduct. In daily work that means you do not hide a risk, you do not invent a number, and you say when you are unsure. This lab is not legal advice.

facts.title: Estimation
facts.text: Estimation is on the technique list. Estimate analysis work separately from build work. Give a range and what would change it. A single point estimate pretends certainty you do not have.

facts.title: Risk and response
facts.text: Write probability only if you have a basis. Otherwise use a simple high, medium, or low and say it is a judgment. Assign a response: avoid, reduce, transfer, or accept. Accepted risks need an owner.

facts.title: RFP and vendor selection
facts.text: A request for proposal should be traceable to requirements. Weight the criteria before you see the responses. Keep a record of questions and answers sent to every bidder. Vendor assessment is the related technique.

facts.title: Build, buy, or configure
facts.text: The design-options task asks you to compare ways to satisfy the need. Include doing nothing. A demo is an input, not a decision. Record why the other options lost.

facts.title: Success measures
facts.text: Define measures before build, so the team cannot move the goal after the result is known. Include a measure that would tell you to roll back.

facts.title: Working backwards
facts.text: Amazon's leadership principles page opened. A press-release-and-FAQ habit is associated with Amazon in public writing, but the book and the internal template were not opened in this check, so the steps are not copied. Use the principles page for what Amazon publishes, and mark any PR/FAQ outline you did not read as unknown. To be confirmed: A primary source for the PR/FAQ template that this check can quote.

facts.title: Operational requirements
facts.text: The Google SRE book introduction treats running the system as part of the engineering problem. Availability, on-call, and failure communication are requirements when a person depends on the service. Write them with the functional behavior.

facts.title: Role names
facts.text: Titles you will see include business analyst, junior or senior business analyst, lead, product owner, and business systems analyst. A title is not a promise of scope. Read the decisions the role owns.

facts.title: Levels, without pay
facts.text: A foundation level practices elicitation and clear writing with support. A working level runs a workstream. A senior level sets the analysis approach and coaches others. This lab states no salaries and no 'typical' pay.

facts.title: STAR, as a structure
facts.text: Situation, task, action, result is a way to answer a behavioral question without wandering. The result should be something you can point to: a decision, a reduced defect, a baseline. Do not invent a metric for the story.

facts.title: Question bank
facts.text: Practice questions: tell us about a stakeholder who disagreed; how you traced a change; how you knew a requirement was testable; how you handled a missing data source. Answer from work you did. Mark practice stories as practice.

facts.title: Case interview
facts.text: A case gives you a short brief and too little time. Restate the need, name stakeholders, ask two clarifying questions, then outline scope, risks, and a first model. Say what you are assuming.

facts.title: Portfolio pieces
facts.text: Three honest pieces beat a large invented program. A requirement set with acceptance criteria, a process model of a public or personal workflow, and a traceability sample are enough. Remove any private data.

facts.title: Resume words
facts.text: Use words you can defend in the interview: elicitation, stakeholder map, user story, acceptance criteria, BPMN, traceability, UAT, workshop. Do not list a tool you have not opened.

facts.title: Contracting notes
facts.text: Corp-to-corp and similar arrangements are commercial structures. The IRS page on independent contractor status opened. Classification is a facts-and-circumstances question. This note is not tax or legal advice.

facts.title: Sponsorship
facts.text: Whether an employer will sponsor a work visa is the employer's decision and a legal question. Nothing in this lab promises sponsorship or a visa outcome, and this note is not legal advice. The USCIS H-1B page opened on 16 October 2026. It describes a specialty occupation as work that applies a body of highly specialized knowledge and that normally requires a bachelor's or higher degree in a directly related specialty. The petitioner files the petition. Specialty-occupation petitions need a certified labor condition application. The same page showed fee alerts that were in flux, including a note about litigation, so this lab does not quote a fee as settled. To be confirmed: Which fee applies to a given petition. Read the live USCIS page before anyone files.

facts.title: Toward product ownership
facts.text: A path some analysts take is deeper discovery, outcome metrics, and backlog accountability. The Scrum Guide and the CSPO page are the public anchors in this lab. Course fees that did not render stay unknown.

facts.title: ECBA
facts.text: Entry Certificate in Business Analysis. The product page describes a bundle at $395 or less that includes membership, the exam, a practice exam, and a learning journey. Student rates are described as $315 or less, depending on region. FAQ: no specific eligibility requirements to sit the exam. Candidates must agree to the code of ethical conduct and the certification terms. Fees table, application column: Not required.

facts.title: CCBA
facts.text: Certification of Capability in Business Analysis, aimed at practitioners with a few years of experience. FAQ: 21 professional-development hours in the last four years. FAQ: 3,750 hours of business analysis work in the last seven years, aligned to the knowledge areas, with minimums across areas as the FAQ details.

facts.title: CBAP
facts.text: Certified Business Analysis Professional, for experienced practitioners. FAQ and CBAP page: 7,500 hours in the last 10 years, and 35 professional-development hours in the last four years. FAQ: at least 900 hours in each of four of the six knowledge areas, at least 3,600 of the 7,500.

facts.title: AAC
facts.text: IIBA Agile Analysis Certification. The product page says $405 or less, including membership and the exam. FAQ: no prerequisites for the specialty certifications. Two years in the specialty are recommended, not required. Fees table: application not required. Exam cell $405 with the line Members $250. Rewrite cell $195 with the line Non-Members $350. Recertification cell $30 with the line Non-Members $50.

facts.title: CBDA
facts.text: Certification in Business Data Analytics. The page lists six blueprint domains. Domains on the CBDA page: research questions 20%, source data 15%, analyze data 16%, interpret and report 20%, influence decisions 20%, guide organization strategy 9%. FAQ: no prerequisites. Two years in the specialty are recommended, not required.

facts.title: PMI-PBA
facts.text: PMI Professional in Business Analysis. The page describes experience paths and the exam shape. It does not show an exam fee in the text that loaded. Set A: secondary degree, 60 months of business analysis in the last 8 years, 35 contact hours. Set B: bachelor's degree or higher, 36 months in the last 8 years, 35 contact hours.

facts.title: Business analysis
facts.text: The practice of understanding a need and shaping a valuable change.

facts.title: Business analyst
facts.text: A person who performs business analysis, whatever the job title.

facts.title: Need
facts.text: A problem or opportunity to be addressed.

facts.title: Stakeholder
facts.text: A person or group with a relationship to the change.

facts.title: Requirement
facts.text: A usable representation of a need, ready for further work.

facts.title: Design
facts.text: A usable representation of a solution.

facts.title: Constraint
facts.text: A limit on the solution that the team does not choose.

facts.title: Assumption
facts.text: A belief treated as true for now, still to be confirmed.

facts.title: Scope
facts.text: The boundary of what is in and out of the change.

facts.title: Elicitation
facts.text: Drawing out information from stakeholders and other sources.

facts.title: Workshop
facts.text: A facilitated session with a purpose and a record.

facts.title: Baseline
facts.text: An agreed version used for later comparison.

facts.title: Traceability
facts.text: A link from a need to requirements, designs, and tests.

facts.title: RTM
facts.text: A requirements traceability matrix: a table of those links.

facts.title: UAT
facts.text: User acceptance testing: a decision against agreed criteria.

facts.title: User story
facts.text: A short statement of role, capability, and outcome.

facts.title: Acceptance criteria
facts.text: The conditions that show a story or requirement is met.

facts.title: Gherkin
facts.text: A language for scenarios using Given, When, and Then.

facts.title: BPMN
facts.text: Business Process Model and Notation, published by OMG.

facts.title: Gateway
facts.text: A BPMN decision point that splits or joins flow.

facts.title: UML
facts.text: Unified Modeling Language, published by OMG.

facts.title: ERD
facts.text: A drawing of entities and the relationships between them.

facts.title: C4
facts.text: A model with system, container, component, and code views.

facts.title: KPI
facts.text: A key performance indicator tied to a decision.

facts.title: HEART
facts.text: Happiness, engagement, adoption, retention, and task success.

facts.title: OKR
facts.text: An objective plus measurable key results.

facts.title: Product backlog
facts.text: The ordered list of what is known to be needed in the product.

facts.title: Increment
facts.text: A concrete step toward the product goal, in Scrum.

facts.title: Product owner
facts.text: An accountability on the Scrum Team for the backlog and value.

facts.title: RACI
facts.text: A matrix of responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed.

facts.title: SWOT
facts.text: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.

facts.title: ADKAR
facts.text: Awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, and reinforcement.

facts.title: Business case
facts.text: A recommendation that shows why a course of action is worth it.

facts.title: Fit-gap
facts.text: A comparison of what a product already does and what the need still requires.

facts.title: Process mining
facts.text: Reconstructing a process from event logs.

facts.title: Non-functional requirement
facts.text: A quality attribute such as speed, security, or availability.

facts.title: CBAP
facts.text: Certified Business Analysis Professional, an IIBA credential.

facts.title: ECBA
facts.text: Entry Certificate in Business Analysis, an IIBA credential.

facts.title: PMI-PBA
facts.text: PMI's Professional in Business Analysis credential.

facts.title: BACCM
facts.text: The Business Analysis Core Concept Model in the BABOK Guide.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Business analysis names a need and a change that has value for a named stakeholder. The public BABOK hub describes a core concept model: change, need, solution, stakeholder, value, and context. A tool name is a solution hypothesis. Write the need in a sentence that still makes sense if the tool changes. Say who decides.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: The same techniques show up in product ownership, project delivery, data work, and change. Shared techniques do not mean shared authority. Ask who decides the need, who decides the date, and who accepts the result. This lab uses the BABOK hub as the core public map and cites neighbors only where a page opened.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: The public contents list six knowledge areas: planning the analysis, elicitation and collaboration, life cycle management, strategy analysis, requirements analysis and design definition, and solution evaluation. Under them sits a long technique list. Learn the question each technique answers. Verification asks if a requirement is fit to use. Validation asks if it is the right one.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: A requirement is a usable representation of a need. Give it an identifier, a source, an owner, and a test. A user story names a role, a capability, and an outcome. Given, When, and Then, from the Gherkin reference, turn the outcome into a scenario. Trace the scenario to a test. Untraced text is a rumor.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Pick the question before the notation. BPMN is for flow: events, activities, gateways. UML is a family of sketches. An ERD names things and relationships. C4 steps from system context to container, component, and code. Stop at the level the audience can use. Draw the unhappy path.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: The 2020 Scrum Guide names three accountabilities and five events, plus the product backlog, sprint backlog, and increment. A kanban board shows flow and limits work in progress. A design sprint is a different sequence: understand, sketch, decide, prototype, test. Do not mix those calendars. Course prices that did not render stay unknown.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: A measure needs a question, a formula, a source, and an owner. HEART, from the cited Google Research paper, is a set of user-centered categories, not a benchmark. SQL, as the PostgreSQL tutorial introduces it, filters and groups rows. Process mining reconstructs paths from event logs you are allowed to use. Leave unknown numbers blank.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Jira, Confluence, Visio, Miro, Lucid, and Figma are places teams keep work. The decision still lives in a sentence a person can accept. Put the outcome and the test on the ticket. Put the decision, the date, and the owner on the page. A polished board with no limit is still a list.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: A model can draft a list, a scenario, or a first drawing. A person checks every fact against a source, marks unknowns, and accepts the text before a stakeholder sees it as a requirement. The handoff from a model to a person, in a contact center or a product flow, is itself a requirement. This lab claims no tool expertise for anyone.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: The moves stay the same: need, stakeholder, rule, test. The constraints change. Healthcare interoperability has a public overview in HL7 FHIR. Banking, insurance, retail, telecom, and contact centers add their own rules. If a rule was not on a page this lab opened, it is not stated as fact.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Discovery restates the job before the feature. A business case lists options, including do nothing, and only the costs and benefits you can source. Change work names awareness, desire, knowledge, ability, and reinforcement, the words on the Prosci page. Vendor choice weights the criteria before the demos.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Read the fee cell and the eligibility FAQ before you pay. ECBA, CCBA, CBAP, AAC, and CBDA figures in this lab were copied from IIBA pages on 16 October 2026, including member and non-member lines as printed. PMI-PBA experience paths and the exam shape are cited. The exam fee was not on the page that loaded. Scrum.org and the SAFe POPM course page did not yield a fee. Confirm before you pay. This lab states no salaries.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: The one-hour path is eight short stops: display, need and roles, six knowledge areas, one testable requirement, one picture, one delivery frame, one measure, then credentials and practice. Skip the long rooms until the path is done.

facts.text: Cards, a quiz, a sort, a match, a stakeholder interview, a triage, and a BPMN order game. Scores stay in this browser. Questions were written for this lab. They are not retired exam items.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Each drawing answers one question. Read the caption and the source. Download the SVG, the PNG, or a standalone HTML page that keeps the color and the disclaimer.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: A flow is an ordered sequence, not a project plan. The dot moves when motion is allowed. On a phone, or with reduced motion, it stays still. The order of the steps is the lesson.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Each term has a short meaning and a source. Filter the list. If a definition disagrees with the standard you are reading, trust the standard and tell us through the contact form.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Every link in the table was requested in the October 2026 check. A page that did not open is omitted, and the related note says what is still to be confirmed.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Copy an outline into your own notes. Leave unknown lines blank. The files are study scaffolds, not a company's form.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Take an SVG, a PNG, or a standalone HTML diagram. Take cheat sheets as PDF, HTML, and PNG. Take flashcards as PDF, JSON, and HTML. Templates come as DOCX, PDF, and HTML. The deck is PPTX. One zip gathers the files after the images are rendered.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Search looks through notes and glossary meanings in this browser. It does not call a server.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: This room is the legal page: disclaimer, copyright, trademarks, third-party licences, privacy, accessibility, and how to ask for a correction. The notes and drawings are original. Browser speech is the platform voice. three.js is not shipped. No pre-recorded clips were made, because no open local speech engine was on the build machine.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: The top-left button slides the menu in. Start here is the short path. The monkey docks on the right edge, can read a section aloud, and can point at an export. The Downloads page lists every standalone file.

facts.title: Learn it in 5 minutes
facts.text: Show a traced requirement, a confirmed model, and a measure with an owner. Practice STAR with a generic story, never a borrowed biography. Pay is not discussed here. Sponsorship is an employer decision and a legal question. The USCIS H-1B page opened for a high-level description of specialty occupations. It is not advice, and this lab promises no visa.

course.title: What this lab is
course.text: Set the display the way you want to read. The lab is free, cited, and silent about pay.

course.title: Need, value, and roles

There are no specific eligibility requirements to sit the exam

choices: 3,750 hours in the last seven years
quizzes.why: The FAQ states 3,750 hours within the last seven years, plus 21 professional-development hours.

quizzes.q: The CBAP exam page states the exam is:
quizzes.why: The CBAP page says 120 questions and 210 minutes. The 130/180 figure on this list matches the CCBA page instead.

quizzes.why: The exam cell shows $395 and notes that student rates are available. The product page also says $395 or less.

choices: A fee only, with no learning
quizzes.why: The page says holders need 60 professional development units in each three-year cycle.

quizzes.why: Cucumber's Gherkin reference uses Given, When, and Then for scenarios.

quizzes.why: The C4 site names software system, container, component, and code.

quizzes.why: Those three artifacts are in the guide's contents.

quizzes.q: ADKAR, on the Prosci page, stands for words that include:
quizzes.why: The Prosci page uses those five words.

quizzes.q: A requirement with no test and no source is best marked:
choices: Unknown until it is traced and made testable
quizzes.why: Traceability and testable acceptance are the habits this lab teaches. Do not approve a gap.

quizzes.q: This lab's rule on salaries is:
quizzes.why: The lab states no salaries and does not repeat vendor pay claims.

Not described, because the readable body asked for authorization

quizzes.why: The IEEE Task Force on Process Mining is the public pointer used here. Mining reconstructs flow from logs.

quizzes.q: When a model drafts a requirement, the accountable person is:
choices: The business analyst who accepts the text
quizzes.why: The analyst owns the requirement. A draft is not an approval.

quizzes.q: The CCBA exam page states:
quizzes.why: The CCBA page says 130 multiple-choice questions and 180 minutes.

quizzes.q: A baseline is:
choices: An agreed version you can compare later
quizzes.why: Without an agreed version, change control has nothing to diff.

quizzes.q: A tool name in a requirement is best treated as:
quizzes.why: The need should still make sense if the tool changes.

quizzes.q: Shared techniques across roles mean:
choices: The project manager owns the need
quizzes.why: Technique overlap is not decision overlap.

quizzes.q: Validation asks whether a requirement is:
quizzes.why: Verification asks whether it is fit to use. Validation asks whether it is the right one.

quizzes.q: Given, When, and Then are how you:

quizzes.q: An unlabeled BPMN path is:
quizzes.why: Every gateway path needs a label.

quizzes.q: The 2020 Scrum Guide's artifacts include:
choices: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment
quizzes.why: Those three are in the guide.

quizzes.q: A KPI without an owner is:
quizzes.why: Name the question, formula, source, and owner.

quizzes.q: A ticket is done when:
quizzes.why: The tool stores the decision. The scenario is the test.

quizzes.q: Who accepts a model draft as a requirement?
quizzes.why: Unreviewed model text is not a requirement.

quizzes.q: When a domain rule was not on an opened page, you:

narration: Welcome. This is a free study lab for business analysis. Start with what the work is, then the six knowledge areas, then a testable requirement. Prices are copied only from pages opened in October 2026. Anything missing is marked to be confirmed. Nothing here is sold, and this lab states no salaries.
